Band-wise reconstruction-error contribution: when an anomaly is detected, the system does not output only an overall anomaly score but also analyzes in which frequency band (or band around a mode) a large reconstruction error occurred. A band's contribution is computed as “that band's reconstruction error ÷ total reconstruction error.” SHAP is kept as an optional feature that can additionally be applied to a separate auxiliary model, and the default method of explanation is the band-wise reconstruction-error contribution.
r1-p07-002: 6. Output and precision-inspection alerts: when the anomaly score exceeds the threshold, an alarm is raised. The alert outputs the anomaly score, a comparison of anomaly scores before and after temperature/humidity compensation, the main contributing frequency band or band around a mode, the rate of change in the first natural frequency, the band-wise reconstruction-error contributions, and an interpretation for inspectors.

r1-p09-003: This section presents the results of applying the proposed anomaly-detection pipeline to the openLAB research-bridge monitoring dataset [8] published in TU Dresden's research data repository (OPARA). openLAB is a full-scale research bridge built in Bautzen, Saxony, Germany: a three-span prestressed concrete bridge about 45 m long. The dataset was collected for about nine months, from February to October 2024, in the undamaged reference state, and provides event-triggered acceleration together with air temperature, humidity and solar radiation, so environmental variation from seasonal change and daily temperature ranges accumulates in it. Because the whole period is undamaged, every alarm exceeding the threshold can be interpreted as a false alarm, which makes the dataset well suited to quantifying the change in false-alarm rate due to environmental compensation. In the analysis, vibration features were extracted from the acceleration records as in 2.3 and linked to the air-temperature and humidity data by time. The normal samples were split in time order into 263 for training and 263 for evaluation, the anomaly threshold was set at the 99th percentile of the training reconstruction error, and three models — uncompensated AE, temperature-compensated AE and temperature/humidity-compensated AE — were compared under identical conditions. The results for each model are shown in the table below.
r1-p09-012: All three models had a training anomaly rate of 0.011 (about 1.1%), consistent with setting the threshold at the 99th percentile of the training reconstruction error. Because the entire evaluation period is in the undamaged reference state, every threshold exceedance is a false alarm. The false-alarm rate was 1.90% for the uncompensated AE and 1.52% for the temperature-compensated and temperature/humidity-compensated AEs. The reduction,
r1-p09-013: 0.38 points, is a small difference — false alarms fell from 5 to 4 out of 263 evaluation samples — so its size is hard to emphasize. Still, on about nine months of full-scale bridge data with accumulated seasonal change and daily temperature ranges, the false-alarm rate moved down rather than up after compensation, so the direction of the temperature/humidity-compensation effect is consistent with our own model-bridge experiment. Adding humidity as a compensation variable did not lower the false-alarm rate below 1.52%, suggesting that the variation in openLAB's vibration characteristics over that period is explained mainly by temperature. The effect of humidity compensation was confirmed in our own model-bridge experiment, where the false-alarm rate in the humidity-change segment fell from 17.5% to 9.1%; that result is presented in 3.4.
r1-p09-014: This saturation of the improvement with temperature compensation alone is consistent with prior work [2], which reported that a bridge's natural frequency varies with temperature even without damage. A limitation is that openLAB's acceleration records are event-triggered, so the excitation source and amplitude differ from record to record and amplitude-dependent features vary greatly. Nevertheless, these differences in excitation act equally on all three models and the reconstruction-error procedure is identical, so the difference in false-alarm rate with and without compensation can be interpreted consistently.
r1-p10-001: The tests have two purposes. First, to examine, with a self-built model bridge and low-cost sensors, how changes in mass distribution affect the vibration features and anomaly scores. The model bridge uses an ADXL355Z-based 3-axis MEMS accelerometer, a DHT22 temperature/humidity sensor and a Raspberry Pi 3 Model A+, with three mass conditions: 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1. This verifies whether low-cost sensors can collect and analyze vibration changes in structural conditions that differ from the normal baseline.
r1-p10-002: Second, to verify the effect of temperature/humidity compensation. The uncompensated, temperature-compensated and temperature/humidity-compensated models are applied with the same procedure to the openLAB dataset (see 2.7), public data from a full-scale bridge, to confirm first at real-bridge scale that environmental compensation reduces false alarms, and then to verify whether a similar trend of improvement is reproduced when the same compensation and detection pipeline is applied to data from our own model-bridge experiment. The openLAB analysis is thus not a separate plan replacing the model experiment but a reference comparison showing that the system's environmental-compensation method works consistently on both full-scale bridge data and our own experimental data; its process and results are presented in 2.7.
r1-p10-004: In the model-bridge experiment, real cracking or corrosion is not reproduced directly; instead, non-destructive changes in mass distribution are created with 10 g weights. Ten 10 g weights are stacked to make a 100 g load at each point, and up to twenty are used in the 1-1 condition, which uses both the left and right points. With the full length of the model bridge L, the left load point is set near x = L/4 and the right near x = 3L/4. Since the ADXL355Z accelerometer is attached at mid-span, x = L/2, the weights are placed so that they do not press on the sensor directly. There are three measurement conditions: 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1. 0-0 is the normal baseline with no weights, 1-0 adds 100 g to the left section, and 1-1 adds 100 g to each of the left and right sections. Because a single load on the right is structurally close to symmetric with the left condition, the single left load 1-0 is used as the representative condition. This experiment is interpreted not as a definitive reproduction of real cracking, corrosion or fatigue damage, but as a structural-condition test to see how the natural frequency, RMS, band energies and Autoencoder reconstruction error change with the mass distribution.
r1-p10-005: This analysis focuses on the data actually collected for the 100 g conditions 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1. If follow-up experiments judge that the change in peak frequency or anomaly score under the 100 g conditions is not large enough, an extended experiment raising the left and right loads to 200 g can be added. The extended experiment is not included in this analysis and is left as a future improvement.
r1-p10-014: Each experimental condition is recorded as left-right (0-0/1-0/1-1), where A is the left section and B the right section. In the basic experiment each digit is 0 = 0 g, 1 = 100 g, and the extended experiment additionally uses 2 = 200 g. For example, 0-0 is the normal baseline with no weights, and 1-0 is the state with 100 g on the left section only.
r1-p11-001: The data-acquisition program is configured to record x-, y- and z-axis acceleration from the ADXL355Z-based accelerometer at 200 Hz and temperature and relative humidity from the DHT22 at about 2-second intervals. Acceleration and temperature/humidity are saved in one file with the same elapsed-time value (ms) measured from the start of recording, so in analysis the vibration features extracted per time window can be linked by time to the mean temperature and mean relative humidity of that window.
r1-p11-002: Raw data are saved as CSV with columns for elapsed time (ms), DHT22 temperature and relative humidity, ADXL355Z internal temperature and 3-axis acceleration in g, and the left/right load condition and repetition number are recorded as per-file metadata. In analysis, per-axis vibration features (RMS, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, spectral entropy, peak frequency and power, band energies) are computed for each time window and linked to that window's mean temperature/humidity and load/environmental condition, and the peak frequency is used as the estimate of the first natural frequency.
r1-p11-004: Testing is divided into analysis of the public openLAB data and our own model-bridge experiment. Because the entire measurement period of the openLAB data (see 2.7) is in the undamaged reference state, every threshold exceedance can be interpreted as a false alarm, allowing a direct comparison of the reduction in false alarms due to environmental compensation. The openLAB analysis compares the anomaly scores and threshold-exceedance rates of the uncompensated, temperature-compensated and temperature/humidity-compensated Autoencoders to confirm at real-bridge scale that environmental compensation reduces false alarms; the detailed process and results are presented in 2.7. Our own model-bridge experiment checks low-cost sensor data acquisition and the ability to detect changes in mass distribution, and verifies whether the compensation effect seen in the openLAB analysis is reproduced on our own data with the same pipeline.
r1-p11-005: The model-bridge experiment uses the ADXL355Z-based accelerometer and the DHT22 sensor. The ADXL355Z is attached at the mid-span position set in 2.2, and the DHT22 is installed beside the bridge in the same environment. The measurement targets are three mass-distribution conditions, 0-0, 1-0 and 1-1; in each condition, vibration is applied in the same way and acceleration and temperature/humidity are recorded for at least 20–30 seconds, repeated three or more times where possible. RMS, standard deviation, peak-to-peak, peak frequency, peak power, band energies and spectral entropy are extracted from the collected signals. Analysis was performed on a MacBook Pro (Apple M3 Max, 36 GB RAM, macOS 26) with Python 3.13, NumPy 2.3 and pandas 2.3, using acceleration sampled at 200 Hz, 4-second analysis windows (800 samples per window) and measurement CSV files for 9 conditions in total.
r1-p11-006: Initially, 12 conditions were planned, combining 3 mass conditions with 4 environmental conditions. However, the temperature-centered condition performed outdoors had a small temperature rise or was accompanied by humidity changes, so it could hardly be regarded as an independent temperature-change condition. The environmental conditions were therefore fixed at three — baseline environment (temperature and humidity not changed artificially), humidity-centered change, and simultaneous temperature/humidity change — and the results were organized around the 9 relatively reliable conditions combining these with the 3 mass conditions (0-0, 1-0, 1-1). The outdoor temperature-change data are used only as supplementary observations.
r1-p11-007: In analysis, the temperature/humidity compensation regression and the anomaly-detection model are trained only on data from the normal baseline condition 0-0, and the remaining conditions, including 1-0 and 1-1, are used only for evaluation. The anomaly threshold is set at the 99th percentile of the normal reconstruction error and applied identically to the uncompensated, temperature-compensated and temperature/humidity-compensated models, so that the compensation methods are compared fairly on the same basis.
r1-p11-009: In the 0-0 condition without weights, the normal baseline vibration pattern is expected to appear relatively stably. In 1-0, 100 g is added to the left section, so the mass distribution becomes asymmetric; in 1-1, a total of 200 g is added on both sides, so the effect of the overall mass increase is expected to be larger.
